summary: Louis-Mathieu Langlès (1763–1824) worked in Indology and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at the Collège de France under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He was Professor of Persian at the Collège de France and founded and administered INALCO.

Louise Allison Cort (b. 1944) works in Japanology and history and archaeology. She studied at Simmons University and St Hugh's College (1966–1969), and served as Curator of Ceramics for the Freer and Sackler Galleries from circa 1981 to 2020.
Louise Child works in religious studies. She earned her PhD at the University of Leeds, where she also taught, and studied under the traditional teacher Ringu Tulku.

Loukram Ibempishak Devi works in Buddhist studies and philosophy. She earned her PhD at Gauhati University under Sibnath Sarma (attested 1999) and also studied under S. Shyamkishor Singh and S. Lokendrajit Singh.
Lozang Samten studied under Tenzin Gyatso and Trijang Rinpoche.
Lozang Tenpa studied under Tenzin Gyatso and Trijang Rinpoche.
Luboš Bělka (b. 1958) is a scholar in religious studies, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology. He studied at Masaryk University from circa 1978 to 1983 and held a post there circa 1993.

Luca Maria Olivieri (b. 1962) specializes in archaeology and Indology. He completed his doctorate at the Free University of Berlin (~2006–2010), directed the Italian Institute for the Middle and Far East (~2013), and joined Ca' Foscari University in 2019.

Lucia Dolce works in Buddhist studies, Japanology, and religious studies. She served as a Lecturer in Japanese Religions (attested 2003–2007) and associate professor (attested 2015) at SOAS University of London.
Lucia Galli is a Tibetologist. She completed her doctorate at the University of Oxford and held a post there.

Lucian Scherman (1864–1946) was an Indologist who studied at Breslau under Adolf Friedrich Stenzler and Munich under Ernst Kuhn. He served as professor at the University of Munich (1893–1916) and as curator and director of the Museum Fünf Kontinente (1907).

Luciano Petech (1914–2010) was a scholar of Tibetology, history and archaeology, and Sinology who studied under Giuseppe Tucci. He held the Chair of History of Eastern Asia at Sapienza University of Rome (1955–1984) and taught at IsMEO.

Lucien Lévy-Bruhl (1857–1939) worked in philosophy and religious studies. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure and the Sorbonne, founded the University of Paris, and taught there from circa 1899 to 1927.

Lucien Tesniere (1893–1954) was a linguist who studied under Antoine Meillet at Paris, Leipzig, and École des langues orientales. He held academic posts at the University of Ljubljana (~1921–1924), University of Strasbourg (1924–1937), and University of Montpellier (1937).
Lucy Annette Jones works in Tibetology and religious studies. She earned her PhD at Rice University under Anne C. Klein and Edith Wyschogrod, and studied under Tenzin Wangyal Rinpoche in 1996–1997.

Ludo Rocher (1926–2016) was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Ghent University and SOAS. He was Professor of Comparative Philology and Sanskrit at Université libre de Bruxelles (1959–1966) and served as Chair at the University of Pennsylvania (1966–2002).

Ludwig Alsdorf (1904–1978) was an Indologist and linguist. He earned his PhD at Hamburg under Walther Schubring and completed his habilitation at Berlin under Heinrich Lüders. He held posts at Berlin, Münster, and Allahabad, and held a chair at Hamburg (1950–1972).

Ludwig Diestel (1825–1879) was a scholar in religious studies and linguistics who studied under Heinrich Ewald. He held posts at the universities of Bonn (~1858–1862), Greifswald (~1862–1867), Jena (~1867–1872), and Tübingen (~1872–1879).

Ludwig Heller (1866–1945) was an Indologist and linguist. He studied under Franz Kielhorn at Göttingen and completed his habilitation at Greifswald, where he became an extraordinary professor in 1904. He also held a post at Tartu in 1918.

Ludwig Lange (1825–1885) was a scholar in philosophy who studied at Göttingen under Theodor Benfey and at Leipzig. He held academic posts at Göttingen (~1847–1853), Charles University (~1853–1859), Giessen (~1859–1871), and Leipzig (~1871–1885).
